hero.h1: The thing you don't do any more
hero.lede: A cloud rather than a camp, because this is not a tense. It is one fixed form that lives only in the past and always says the same thing: this was true, and it is not any more. The gap between the block and NOW is not empty space — it is the meaning.

sections.label: Cloud briefing
sections.title: When to use it
sections.lead: This is not a tense. It is one fixed form that exists only in the past and always means the same thing: this was true, and it is not true now. The gap between the block and NOW is the entire point of saying it.

cards.head: A habit that has stopped
cards.body: Something you did regularly and do not do any more.

cards.head: A state that has changed
cards.body: Not an action at all — a way things were.
cards.ex: "There used to be a bakery on this corner."

cards.head: Repeated over a stretch of years
cards.body: The years are vague on purpose; do not date them.
cards.ex: "We used to walk to school every day."

cards.head: The contrast is the message
cards.body: You are not reporting the past. You are pointing at the change.

cards.head: Only ever the past
cards.body: There is no present form. For a present habit, use the present simple.
cards.ex: "I drink coffee." not "I use to drink coffee."

cards.head: Careful with the missing d
cards.body: The d vanishes after did, exactly as in any past question.

cards.head: Never changes
cards.body: No person, no number, no -s. One form for everybody.

charts.head: Where the d goes
charts.note: The only spelling difficulty in the whole form. Did already carries the past, so the verb behind it drops back to its plain form — use, not used. It is the same rule as did you want, not did you wanted.

head: Form
Spelling
Example
rows: This is the commonest written error.

charts.head: Used to or would?
charts.note: Both can tell you about the old days, and they are not interchangeable. Would handles repeated actions; it cannot handle states. Used to handles both, which makes it the safer choice.

head: Meaning
used to
would
rows: Common in writing: "Every summer we would…"

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with this form is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: I used to play tennis. / I play tennis.
There is no present use to. Decide which you mean.
I didn't used to like it.
I didn't use to like it.
Did carries the past, so the d comes off.
I used to live here for ten years.
I lived here for ten years.
A stated length of time makes it a fact, not a contrast. Past simple.

sections.label: The fork in the path
sections.title: Used to or past simple?

charts.note: Both are past and both are true. The difference is what you are drawing attention to: the past simple reports, and used to points at the change.

head: Question
used to
Past simple
rows:
Contrasting then with now.
"I used to live in Rome."

Reporting a fact.
"I lived in Rome for two years."
Never. "I used to break my leg" is nonsense.

charts.example: The pair that shows it: "I lived in Rome for two years" tells you where I was. "I used to live in Rome" tells you where I am not. Same past, entirely different point.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Words that push you to past simple

sections.example: A useful habit: say the sentence and then add … but not any more. If that sounds redundant rather than wrong, used to is the right form.

sections.label: Interactive
sections.title: The block, and the gap after it

diagram.intro: The slate block is what was true. The red line is where it stopped, and it stops hard — this form has no soft ending. What matters most is the empty dashed box: the stretch between the block and NOW where the thing is simply not true any more. That gap is what you are actually communicating when you say used to. Click either to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: Then — what used to be true
items: There used to be a bakery on this corner.
We used to walk to school every day.

quiz.prompt: I _____ smoke, but I gave up ten years ago.
quiz.explain: A stopped past habit takes used to, with the d.

quiz.prompt: There _____ be a bakery on this corner.
quiz.explain: Used to handles states as well as actions. Would cannot: there would be a bakery is wrong.

quiz.prompt: I _____ like coffee when I was a child.
quiz.explain: Did already carries the past, so the d comes off: didn't use to.
Did + use to, with no d. This is the commonest written error in the whole form.

quiz.prompt: I _____ in Rome for two years.
quiz.hint: There is a length of time here.
quiz.explain: A stated duration makes it a plain past fact, so the past simple. Used to would lose the point.

quiz.prompt: We _____ to school every day when we were small.
quiz.explain: A repeated past action that has stopped: used to walk. Would walk would also work here.

quiz.hint: Is this the past at all?
quiz.explain: There is no present used to. A present habit is simply the present simple.
Used to needs something repeated or continuous. One event takes the past simple.

quiz.prompt: Every summer we _____ swim in the lake.
quiz.hint: A repeated action in a story.
quiz.explain: For repeated past actions, would is a natural alternative to used to, especially in writing.

quiz.prompt: There _____ be a cinema here, but they knocked it down.
quiz.explain: Would cannot carry a state. Used to can, which is why it is the safer form.
Have here is a state, so would is out. Used to says: he doesn't now.

quiz.prompt: I _____ get up at five when I worked on the farm.
quiz.explain: A stopped past habit. Was used to would mean it did not bother me, which is a different sentence.

quiz.prompt: They _____ own a boat, but they sold it.
quiz.explain: Own is a state verb, so would is impossible. Used to carries both the past and the change.

quiz.prompt: _____ he _____ smoke before he met you?
quiz.explain: Did + use to. Was he used to smoking would ask something else entirely.

results: Clean run. You know where the d goes and when the past simple is the better sentence.
Solid progress. Worth a look at the other cloud before you go on.
Good first attempt. The missing d is the part to read again.
